narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the bottom decile. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your first-year ranking worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. At the 6th decile, you matched the average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance about your early academic ability.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and increased the predicted risk of failure. Your score of 26.5 sits well below the 37.2 average among accepted applicants, which the model interpreted as an indicator of weaker preparation for the exam.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of your low third-year performance and below-average LSAT outweighed your solid first-year results.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also considering a post-baccalaureate program or intensive bar-prep coursework to demonstrate improved academic capability before reapplying.
